extracted.intended_audience: school administrators, Title IX coordinators, athletic directors, postsecondary and K-12 policymakers, and other stakeholders drafting or applying athletic eligibility policies under Title IX
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory standards for when and how recipients (schools, districts, postsecondary institutions) may adopt or apply sex-related criteria that would limit or deny a student's eligibility to participate on a male or female athletic team consistent with their gender identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial Relationship Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex-related criteria that would limit or deny a student's eligibility to participate on a male or female team consistent with their gender identity must be, for each sport, level of competition, and grade or education level, 'substantially related' to achieving an important educational objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation requires a 'direct, substantial relationship between' the recipient's objective and the means used (citing Miss. Univ. for Women v. Hogan). Courts interpret this to preclude mechanical application of stereotypes and demand an evidentiary, tailored connection between means and objectives (see Virginia, Hecox, Clark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Important Educational Objective Requirement (e.g., fairness or injury prevention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any sex-related eligibility criteria limiting participation consistent with gender identity must be justified by an important educational objective, such as fairness in competition or prevention of sports-related injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness in competition and injury prevention are recognized as potentially important objectives, but the recipient must show the criteria are substantially related to achieving that objective for the specific sport/level/grade. Case examples: Clark (upholding exclusion in specific context), and references to stakeholder feedback and existing §106.41(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: No Reliance on Overbroad Generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria must not rely on overly broad generalizations about the talents, capacities, or preferences of male and female students (for example, assuming all transgender girls have an unfair competitive advantage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorical exclusions of all transgender girls/women from female teams would fail because they are one-size-fits-all approaches that ignore sport-, level-, and grade-specific differences (citing Hecox; Virginia). Evidence must support any asserted generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sport-Specific Substantial Relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Any sex-related eligibility criteria must be substantially related to an important educational objective for each particular sport to which they apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because sports vary in rules and the skills they prioritize, the analysis must account for the nature of the particular sport (Javits Amendment and Att'y Gen. v. Mass. Interscholastic Athletic Ass'n). The regulation does not necessarily require distinct criteria for every sport, but criteria must satisfy the standard as applied to that sport; overbroad, sport-agnostic assumptions are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level-of-Competition Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex-related criteria must be substantially related to achieving an important educational objective for each level of competition to which they apply (e.g., intramural, junior varsity, varsity, elite/college).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must account for distinctions between lower levels prioritizing broad participation and higher levels involving selective, elite competition (examples: USA Gymnastics permitting participation below elite level; World Athletics limiting some rules to world-ranking/elite levels). Criteria are more likely to satisfy the rule at higher competition levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grade or Education Level Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex-related eligibility criteria must, for each grade or education level, be substantially related to the achievement of an important educational objective, recognizing developmental differences across ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must account for developmental factors, harms from exclusion, athletic skill development, and legal status (minor vs adult). The Department believes few, if any, sex-related eligibility criteria could comply when applied to elementary students; it will be particularly difficult immediately after elementary school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm Minimization Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a recipient adopts or applies sex-related criteria that would limit or deny participation consistent with gender identity, it must do so in a way that minimizes harms to the affected students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harms include forced disclosure of transgender status, trauma, invasion of privacy, embarrassment, harassment, and loss of opportunity. Even criteria that are substantially related to an objective violate the proposed rule if the recipient can reasonably adopt or apply less harmful alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Least Restrictive Alternate Means / Consideration of Alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the objective could be accomplished through alternative criteria that would not limit or deny a student's participation consistent with their gender identity is relevant; if so, using more restrictive sex-related criteria may be pretextual and impermissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts compare whether goals can be achieved through other means (e.g., Virginia Military Institute adjustments). The Department expects recipients to consider and prefer alternatives that avoid exclusion or reduce harm when these alternatives are reasonable and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on Reliance on False Assumptions (e.g., misconduct risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may not base exclusionary criteria on false assumptions about transgender students (for example, that transgender students are more likely to engage in inappropriate conduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies excluding students for perceived misconduct risk lack substantial relation if unsupported by evidence (citing Parents for Privacy v. Barr; Doe v. Boyertown). Schools may take nondiscriminatory steps to prevent misconduct and protect privacy for all students, but cannot rest criteria on stereotypes or factual falsehoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of Documentation/Verification Must Minimize Privacy and Access Harms
rubrics_metrics.description: If a recipient uses documentation, verification, or administrative criteria to implement eligibility rules, those processes must be designed to minimize difficulty, invasion of privacy, and disclosure of confidential information for affected students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: documentation requirements aimed at ensuring equal athletic opportunity must avoid unnecessarily burdensome or privacy-invasive procedures. If less-harmful means exist, the more harmful documentation processes are not permitted under the harm-minimization requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-Based, Reasoned Analysis Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Justifications for sex-related eligibility criteria must be based on reasoned analysis and evidence rather than mechanical application of traditional, often inaccurate assumptions or stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes reliance on facts and case-specific evidence (Miss. Univ. for Women; Clark). Policies should demonstrate how the evidence supports the asserted relationship between criteria and the educational objective; conclusory or stereotype-driven rationales will fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to Preserve Overall Equal Athletic Opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must provide overall equal athletic opportunity for students regardless of sex; adopting sex-separate teams is permissible in limited circumstances but does not excuse discriminatory treatment when offering those opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current §106.41(b) permits male/female teams in certain circumstances to promote overall equal opportunity, but recipients remain responsible not to discriminate otherwise. Offering sex-separated teams cannot be used as a blanket justification for policies that impose more-than-de-minimis harms on certain students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Relative Prevalence and Displacement Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing claims that allowing transgender students to participate consistent with gender identity will displace cisgender students, recipients and courts should consider evidence about the very small number of transgender student-athletes and whether displacement is supported by record evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and the Department note that displacement claims are often unsupported; agencies should weigh empirical evidence (e.g., Utah High Sch. Activities Ass'n findings; Hecox) rather than assume displacement will occur.
